title: Declining and Saying No
short: Decline invitations, food and requests kindly and briefly ("Thank you for asking; I can't make it"); a long excuse isn't needed, and a lie isn't either.
trouble: Learners invent elaborate excuses that get caught, or say yes and then don't show. A kind, clear no is both polite and honest.

blocks.html: Like answering a rude remark, declining takes calm and kindness. Invitations, second helpings, favors and requests all sometimes need a no.
Decline invitations, food and requests kindly and briefly: "Thank you for asking; I can't make it." A long excuse isn't needed, and a lie isn't either.

A kind, clear no respects the other person: they can plan, ask someone else or move on. A long excuse invites argument or questions, and an invented one can be found out, which hurts more than the no would have. Saying yes and then not showing up is the worst choice of all, because the other person counted on you. Thanks, a clear answer and warmth are all a no needs.

messages.text: Want to help at the bake sale Saturday morning? We need people from 8 to noon!

choices.text: Thanks for asking! I can't make it Saturday, but I hope it goes great.

choices.why: Saying yes when you can't go leaves the organizer short-handed later.

choices.text: I would, but my aunt's cousin is visiting and my car might need repairs and...
choices.why: A long excuse isn't needed, and it invites questions.

blocks.title: A second helping
blocks.q: At a dinner, the host offers Leo more lasagna. He is full. What does he say?
steps: He thanks the host and the food: "Thank you, it was delicious, but I couldn't eat another bite."
No excuse about diets is needed.
blocks.a: A warm "No, thank you" with a compliment.

blocks.title: A favor at work
blocks.q: A coworker asks Hana to take on a project she has no time for. What can she say?
steps: She thanks him for thinking of her.
"I'm sorry, I can't take that on right now; my plate is full this month."
If she can, she suggests another way to help: "I could look over the plan next week."
blocks.a: A clear, kind no, perhaps with another way to help.
